request: Remind requesters when a ticket has been waiting on them for too long.

labels.why: The lifecycle has no waiting-on-requester state, so the request's core condition has to be defined in this program's terms.
The threshold, the instant it is counted from, and whether it varies by priority are the requested behaviour itself.
How many reminders, how far apart, and when they stop are the reminder's own conduct.
The events that end the waiting are the feature's boundaries; with no reply endpoint the spec must say which existing events count as a response, and needs no new channel to do so.
The reminder's wording, its fields and its recipient (given the free-text requester field) go through the existing templates and outbox.
The reminder has to agree with the existing resolved notice's 'reply within 7 days to reopen it' wording.
The worker's contract requires scheduled work to be a worker job, so where and how the check runs must be settled.
An outbox key deduplicates only while pending and delivery is at-least-once, so avoiding duplicate reminders is correctness rigour.
Re-checking the condition when enqueueing keeps a stale reminder from going out; that is the behaviour's own correctness.
Failure routing through the existing retries, dead state and template rule is the expected rigour.
Whether a backlog of reminders goes out when the feature is first deployed is a deployment step for existing data.
The lifecycle allows resolve, reopen, resolve again, so the reminder timing and keys across cycles are a boundary of the behaviour.

labels.applies_part: The spec must settle what happens at exactly the threshold and which clock and time zone the comparison uses; holding reminders outside business hours, weekends or holidays would need a business calendar the program lacks.
labels.why: The threshold boundary and clock source apply; a business-hours and holiday calendar is a capability nobody asked for.
Persistence names every field it saves and loads, so any new tracking data has to be placed and named.
Data files from the current version must still load, and the load checks must cover the new fields, to preserve the existing program.
Whether a reminder enters the audit log or changes the ticket's updated time affects the existing audit and updated-time rules.

labels.applies_part: The spec must settle that the threshold and the switch are operator settings in the environment and that reminders go out as the system, under the existing X-Actor and internal-network model.
labels.why: Who controls the feature applies; stopping or sending reminders by hand, or any real authorization, needs controls and sign-in the request does not ask for.
Settings follow the existing pattern of validated environment variables, and the rule that WORKER_INTERVAL_MS=0 stops all background work must hold.
Operators see reminders through the existing outbox report and tools, and the CLI's raw column positions must be preserved.
How late a reminder may go out, how many go in one tick, and the check's cost are operational rigour for a job that scans every ticket.
Which existing behaviour must be preserved is explicitly part of what applies.
Tests with the manual clock, doc updates, the changelog and version bump, and a decision record are the conventions CONTRIBUTING requires.
